target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is educationally valuable and ethically acceptable because it uses over-98%-already-deceased animals and fetal pigs that are meat-industry byproducts.
objection: Animal dissection should still be opposed because most dissection animals are caught in the wild, which harms local populations and biodiversity, and because the supply methods are inhumane and environmentally damaging.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is unnecessary because students can learn just as well or better from synthetic models and computer simulations.
objection: Non-animal alternatives cannot fully replicate the tactile, specimen-level learning of real dissection, including direct manipulation of real tissues and exposure to natural specimen variability.

target: AG2’s claim that the absence of an AP Biology or NGSS dissection requirement means dissection should not be used.
objection: Curriculum standards set minimum requirements and do not exhaust the legitimate teaching methods teachers may use, so the lack of an explicit requirement does not justify banning an educationally valuable dissection activity.

target: AG2’s assumption that dissection necessarily depends on animals being newly killed for classroom use.
objection: In typical school dissection programs, the animals are already deceased or are industry byproducts, so dissection does not inherently require killing animals specifically for the classroom.

target: AG2’s argument that because physician training does not rely on student animal dissection, dissection is not needed in biology education.
objection: Biology education has its own educational goals—such as fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, critical thinking, and enthusiasm for science—so the lack of dependence in medical training does not show dissection is unnecessary in school biology.

target: AG1’s claim that using already-deceased or byproduct specimens eliminates the relevant harm objections.
objection: Even if the specimens are already dead or are byproducts, obtaining them still depends on animal exploitation and environmentally damaging supply chains, so serious animal-welfare and environmental costs remain.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection remains unjustified because the sourcing still causes harm.
objection: Because over 98% of dissection animals are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, typical dissection does not newly kill animals for class and can divert byproducts from landfills, so the claimed added harm is not serious enough to bar dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that using already-deceased specimens removes the environmental objection.
objection: Dissection itself commonly uses preservatives such as formaldehyde and produces hazardous chemical waste, so it still creates serious environmental harm even if the animals were not freshly killed for the classroom.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is inherently environmentally harmful because of preservative chemicals and waste.
objection: In properly run school programs, those chemicals and wastes are handled under standard safety procedures and regulated hazardous-waste disposal, so dissection does not inherently cause serious environmental releases.

target: AG2’s claim that school-level safety controls cannot reliably prevent harmful releases.
objection: Schools can condition dissection on trained supervision and compliant hazardous-waste handling, so serious environmental harm is not an unavoidable feature of dissection across typical schools.

target: AG1’s assumption that compliant hazardous-waste handling resolves the moral problem.
objection: Even with proper chemical handling, student animal dissection still uses real animal bodies and therefore continues to involve animal exploitation and animal-welfare harm that compliance does not remove.

target: AG1’s claim that wild-catching is not a major concern because most specimens are already dead or byproducts.
objection: Approximately 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, so dissection predictably harms biodiversity and local populations through sourcing, and that ecological harm is not prevented by classroom safety procedures.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection’s biodiversity harm is substantial despite typical sourcing practices.
objection: Because over 98% of specimens are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, dissection does not primarily rely on wild-caught animals, so biodiversity harm from sourcing is substantially mitigated in typical school practice.

target: AG1’s claim that non-animal alternatives cannot meet the relevant learning goals.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can provide hands-on interaction, support fine-motor practice and hand-eye coordination, and teach critical observation and reasoning without using real animals, so the learning goals can be met without dissection.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives fully replace dissection’s educational value.
objection: Real-animal dissection uniquely gives students direct manipulation and inspection of real tissues and specimen variability, so alternatives do not fully replicate the specific tactile learning mechanism or the related learning and enthusiasm effects.

target: AG1’s assumption that using already-dead/byproduct specimens makes dissection low-harm overall.
objection: Dissection commonly still uses hazardous preservatives and creates hazardous chemical waste, so even with already-deceased specimens the activity can still impose serious environmental harm and is not low-harm overall.

target: AG2’s claim that hazardous-chemical harms defeat the ethical justification for dissection even when specimens are already dead.
objection: Under the proposed ethical standard, the key tradeoff is whether dissection adds meaningful animal death or exploitation for classroom purposes; if it largely does not, and it has educational upside, then dissection can still be justified.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives cannot reliably produce the same learning outcomes or enthusiasm as dissection.
objection: High-fidelity synthetic models and simulations can present multiple cases and allow repeated, guided, active exploration of anatomy and function, so they can replicate the relevant learning mechanism closely enough to make dissection unnecessary.

target: AG1’s broader conclusion that real-animal dissection remains justified because it has unique educational upside.
objection: Synthetic models and simulations can teach anatomy at least as well as dead-animal dissection while avoiding animal use, so dissection is not educationally necessary and does not have uniquely required upside.

target: AG2’s claim that the existence of non-animal alternatives makes dissection unjustified despite its benefits.
objection: If dissection delivers substantial educational and career benefits while imposing only low added sourcing harm because the specimens are already dead or byproducts, then the availability of alternatives alone does not make dissection unjustified.

target: AG1’s overall conclusion that dissection is justified because it is educationally useful and not required by standards.
objection: AP Biology and NGSS do not require dissection, synthetic models and simulations can meet the learning goals, and dissection still imposes serious animal-welfare and ecological harms, so requiring students to dissect animals is ethically unjustified.
